summary.text: The counterexample is $n=800322180$: monotonicity bounds both binomial indices by $16$, and a finite check of those pairs shows that each nonnegative remainder after subtracting the two binomial terms has some prime $q\equiv3\pmod4$ occurring to an odd exponent (while the remaining pairs already exceed $n$). Such a remainder cannot be a sum of two squares, since divisibility of $a^2+b^2$ by such a prime forces divisibility of both $a$ and $b$ by that prime, so no representation exists and hence $a(800322180)=0$.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
B(k)=\binom{2k+1}{k}
\]
and set
\[
N=800{,}322{,}180.
\]
We will prove that there are no nonnegative integers \(a,b,c,d\)—even without imposing the ordering conditions \(a\le b\) and \(c\le d\)—such that
\[
a^2+b^2+B(c)+B(d)=N. \tag{1}
\]
It will follow in particular that the number of representations counted by A303639 is zero at \(N\). Since \(N>1\), this disproves the conjecture that every term after the first is positive.

First we record the elementary obstruction to being a sum of two squares that will be used in every finite case.

**Sum-of-two-squares obstruction.** Let \(q\) be a prime with \(q\equiv3\pmod4\). If
\[
q\mid x^2+y^2,
\]
then \(q\mid x\) and \(q\mid y\). Indeed, reduce modulo \(q\). If \(y\not\equiv0\pmod q\), then
\[
(xy^{-1})^2\equiv-1\pmod q.
\]
But \(-1\) is not a quadratic residue modulo a prime congruent to \(3\pmod4\). For example, writing \(q=4m+3\), if \(t^2\equiv-1\), then Fermat's theorem gives
\[
1\equiv t^{q-1}=(t^2)^{(q-1)/2}\equiv(-1)^{2m+1}\equiv-1\pmod q,
\]
a contradiction. Hence \(q\mid y\), and then \(x^2\equiv0\pmod q\), so primality of \(q\) gives \(q\mid x\) as well.

Consequently, if \(x^2+y^2=R\) and \(q\mid R\), then writing \(x=qx_1\) and \(y=qy_1\) gives
\[
R=q^2(x_1^2+y_1^2). \tag{2}
\]
Repeating this argument shows the following familiar necessary condition:

> In a sum of two integer squares, every prime congruent to \(3\pmod4\) occurs with even exponent.

For completeness, if the exact exponent of such a prime \(q\) in \(R\) were an odd number \(2r+1\), applying (2) \(r\) times would produce a sum of two squares divisible by \(q\) but not by \(q^2\). The preceding argument says that its two square roots are both divisible by \(q\), forcing divisibility by \(q^2\), a contradiction.

We next bound the possible binomial indices. Direct calculation gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrr}
k&0&1&2&3&4&5&6&7\\ \hline
B(k)&1&3&10&35&126&462&1716&6435
\end{array}
\]
and
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrr}
k&8&9&10&11&12&13&14&15\\ \hline
B(k)&24310&92378&352716&1352078&5200300&20058300&77558760&300540195.
\end{array} \tag{3}
\]
The next value is
\[
B(16)=\binom{33}{16}=1{,}166{,}803{,}110>N. \tag{4}
\]
These values can be obtained successively from
\[
\frac{B(k+1)}{B(k)}
 =\frac{(2k+3)(2k+2)}{(k+1)(k+2)}
 =\frac{2(2k+3)}{k+2}.
\]
This ratio is greater than \(1\) for every \(k\ge0\), so \(B(k)\) is strictly increasing. It follows from (4) that if either \(c\ge16\) or \(d\ge16\), then the corresponding binomial term by itself is greater than \(N\), making (1) impossible because all four terms in (1) are nonnegative. Thus only
\[
0\le c,d\le15 \tag{5}
\]
need be considered.

Because \(B(c)+B(d)\) is symmetric in \(c,d\), it is enough to consider \(c\le d\). For each pair in (5), put
\[
R_{c,d}=N-B(c)-B(d).
\]
If (1) held, then
\[
a^2+b^2=R_{c,d}. \tag{6}
\]
The following table supplies, for every \(0\le c\le d\le15\), a prime factor of \(R_{c,d}\) that is congruent to \(3\pmod4\) and occurs to an odd exponent. In row \(c\), the entries correspond in order to \(d=c,c+1,\ldots,15\). An entry \(q^e\) means that \(q^e\) exactly divides \(R_{c,d}\), i.e. \(q^e\mid R_{c,d}\) but \(q^{e+1}\nmid R_{c,d}\). When the superscript is omitted, the exact exponent is \(1\).

\[
\begin{array}{c|llllllllllllllll}
c&\multicolumn{16}{l}{\text{entries for }d=c,c+1,\ldots,15}\\ \hline
0&647&163&67&3&23&467&223&991&7&3&23&3&887&26905651&7&1999\\
1&3^3&643&19&3&3^7&3&3&78607&27594131&3&31&11&3&3&3\\
2&11&3&200080511&23&284003&4326031&19&3&399984727&3&79512187&127&2819&7\\
3&7&7&7&43&5843&3&7923067&7&7&3&23&23&23\\
4&3&3&719&3&563&200057419&3^3&7&7&3&3&3\\
5&3^3&3&3&12504647&23&3&7&7&3&3&3\\
6&3&19&7&7&3&139&227&11&3^5&67\\
7&3&199&31&31&3331&139&3&3&3\\
8&689891&3&223&3&59&11&7591&19990307\\
9&19&887&19&3&11&19&19\\
10&3&19&7&19&3^3&19\\
11&7&3&19&19&19\\
12&7&19&19&19\\
13&3&3&3\\
14&3&3\\
15&3
\end{array} \tag{7}
\]

Here is the finite arithmetic behind the table. One first computes each residual by subtracting two entries of (3) from \(800{,}322{,}180\). Each displayed base \(q\) is prime and has remainder \(3\) upon division by \(4\). Dividing its residual repeatedly by \(q\) gives exactly the exponent displayed in (7), and that exponent is always odd. These assertions are direct integer divisions. Primality of each displayed number is checked by trial division: no integer from \(2\) through its integer square root divides it; this range suffices because every composite integer has a factor no larger than its square root.

To illustrate both the construction of the residuals and the two kinds of entries in the table, consider a few cases. For \((c,d)=(0,0)\),
\[
R_{0,0}=800322180-1-1=800322178,
\]
and \(647\) divides this number while \(647^2\) does not; also \(647\) is prime and \(647\equiv3\pmod4\). For \((c,d)=(0,1)\),
\[
R_{0,1}=800322180-1-3=800322176,
\]
and \(163\) occurs to exact exponent one. For an entry with a larger odd exponent,
\[
R_{1,1}=800322180-3-3=800322174=3^3\cdot29641562,
\]
where the remaining factor is not divisible by \(3\). The other exceptional odd powers in (7) are likewise given by
\[
\begin{aligned}
R_{1,5}&=800321715=3^7\cdot365945,\\
R_{4,10}&=799969338=3^3\cdot29628494,\\
R_{5,5}&=800321256=3^3\cdot29641528,\\
R_{6,14}&=722761704=3^5\cdot2974328,\\
R_{10,14}&=722410704=3^3\cdot26755952,
\end{aligned}
\]
and in each line the displayed cofactor is not divisible by \(3\). Every other table entry has exact exponent one.

We now finish the exclusion. Fix any pair \(c,d\) allowed by (5). Interchange them if necessary so that \(c\le d\), which leaves \(R_{c,d}\) unchanged. The corresponding entry of (7) gives a prime \(q\equiv3\pmod4\) whose exact exponent in \(R_{c,d}\) is odd. By the sum-of-two-squares obstruction, \(R_{c,d}\) cannot equal \(a^2+b^2\) for any integers \(a,b\). This contradicts (6). Thus equation (1) has no solution for indices below \(16\), while (4) and monotonicity excluded every larger index. Hence equation (1) has no solution at all in nonnegative integers.

In particular, there is no solution satisfying the additional restrictions \(a\le b\) and \(c\le d\). Therefore the representation count in A303639 at this integer is
\[
a(800{,}322{,}180)=0.
\]
Since \(800{,}322{,}180>1\), this is a counterexample to the conjecture that \(a(n)>0\) for every \(n>1\).
